**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Time allowed: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section. All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples. Only the required number of questions will be marked. Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Structure of the paper: SECTION A: Physical Geography (questions 1 to 3); SECTION B: Human Geography (questions 4 to 6); SECTION C: Contemporary Environmental and Development Issues (question 7, with an EITHER/OR choice between two sets of sub-questions).

questions.enonce_markdown: (a) Examine **two** benefits and **two** problems associated with plantation farming.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A plantation is a large estate, usually in the tropics, devoted to the commercial production of one cash crop (monoculture) such as rubber, oil palm, banana, tea, sugar cane or cocoa, using capital, paid labour and scientific methods, and usually with a factory on the estate for processing the crop. In Cameroon examples include the Cameroon Development Corporation (CDC: banana, rubber, oil palm and tea in the South West and North West Regions), SOCAPALM (oil palm), HEVECAM (rubber), SOSUCAM (sugar) and the banana plantations of the Njombe-Penja area (PHP).

**Benefits**

1. **Employment, incomes and rural development.** Plantations employ many workers, directly and in transport, processing and services, and give them a regular cash income. Companies often provide housing, schools, health centres, roads and electricity for the workers and for the neighbouring communities, so they develop the rural area (the CDC camps and the towns that grew near plantations are examples). Smallholders ("outgrowers") around them can receive seeds, inputs, technical advice and a guaranteed market.
2. **Export earnings, taxes and industrial linkages.** The crops are mainly exported (bananas, rubber, palm oil, tea), earning **foreign exchange**, taxes and royalties for the government, which pays for national development. Processing (palm oil mills, rubber factories, sugar factories) creates further industries, training and technology transfer (multiplier effect). The large scale permits efficient production, quality control and high yields.

**Problems**

1. **Environmental damage and over-dependence on one crop.** Monoculture removes the natural vegetation (clearing of forest reduces biodiversity), exhausts the soil and encourages erosion and the spread of pests and diseases; heavy use of fertilisers and pesticides pollutes rivers and affects workers' health. The estate and the national economy depend on one crop, so price falls on the world market or a disease bring hardship and unemployment.
2. **Social and land problems.** Large areas of land are taken from local communities, which causes land shortages, conflicts with villagers and loss of land for food crops. Wages are often low, working conditions harsh, and the labour is often migrant, leading to social tensions. Much of the profit goes to foreign owners or the state (leakage of profits), so the local area benefits less than it should.

**Conclusion.** Plantations bring jobs, infrastructure and foreign exchange, but they can damage the environment, create dependence on one export and cause land conflicts; the balance depends on how they are managed (for example by outgrower schemes and fair land agreements).

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) Analyze **three** reasons why present-day industries are becoming more widely dispersed and flexible in their spatial locations.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Early industries (coal, iron and steel, textiles) were tied to raw materials and power, so they were clustered on coalfields and ports. Present-day industries are more **footloose**: free to locate in many more places and to change location, even though there are still industrial clusters. Reasons:

**1. Improvements in transport, energy supply and communication.** The national electricity grid and the use of electricity, oil and gas means that power is available almost everywhere and not only at the coalfield. Better roads, containerisation, air freight and lower transport costs reduce the importance of distance to raw materials and markets. Modern telecommunications and the internet allow firms to manage plants, suppliers and customers in different places and even different countries. This makes dispersal possible.

**2. Changes in the nature of industry and in production methods.** Modern industries such as electronics, computing, pharmaceuticals and assembly of components make **light, high-value products** whose transport costs are a small part of total costs (the raw material is small and not bulky, so the factory can be anywhere). Automation and flexible production systems (small batch production, "just-in-time" delivery from sub-contractors) allow smaller factories to be located in different areas. Firms can subcontract parts to many small firms, and can quickly change what they produce.

**3. Government policy, and the push and pull of different locations.** Governments encourage dispersal to reduce regional inequality, through industrial estates, tax holidays, subsidies, regional development grants and free-trade or industrial free zones (as in some Cameroonian cities, and in many countries), and by planning controls in congested cities. Firms are pushed from the city centres by **congestion, high land and labour costs, pollution and restrictions**, and pulled to smaller towns and rural areas by cheaper land, available (often cheaper) labour, pleasant environments, science parks near universities (such as Cambridge) and motorway corridors (the M4 corridor in England). **Transnational corporations** now also place factories in low-wage developing countries, following cheaper labour and market access.

**Conclusion.** Because energy, transport and communications are available nearly everywhere, products are lighter and production is more flexible, and governments encourage regional development, modern industries are more dispersed and mobile than the traditional heavy industries.

questions.enonce_markdown: (c) Briefly explain why most roads are hardly straight.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In theory the shortest route between two places is a straight line, and a straight road costs least to build and use. In practice, most roads bend because of physical and human factors.

**Physical factors**
1. **Relief.** Roads avoid steep slopes: in hilly and mountainous country they follow contours, wind around hills, or climb in zigzag bends (hairpins) so that the gradient is not too steep for vehicles. The roads up the escarpments of the Western Highlands and the slopes of Mount Cameroon are examples.
2. **Rivers, swamps, lakes and other obstacles.** Roads bend to reach a narrow crossing point, a ford or a bridge site, to avoid marshes and flood plains with weak foundations, large rock outcrops, forests or lakes, because crossing them directly would be costly or impossible.

**Human factors**
3. **Settlements and land use.** Roads are made to link villages and towns on the way, not just the two end points, and they bend to pass round farms, plots, sacred sites and private property (to reduce the cost of buying land and avoid conflict). Many roads began as footpaths and cattle tracks that followed the easiest and most convenient route and were later widened and surfaced.
4. **Cost and safety.** Straight roads over rough ground would need costly cutting, filling, tunnels and bridges; curves reduce construction cost. On a few stretches bends are even introduced to slow traffic.

**Conclusion.** The route of a road is a compromise between the shortest distance and the obstacles of relief, water and settlement, and the cost of construction, which is why most roads are curved.
